title: "Am having a car" → "have a car"
rule: In global English, say "I have" for owning, not "I'm having".

examples.work: I have the new build on my laptop, so I'll run the demo.
examples.everyday: We have a car now, so I can drop you at the station.

insteadOf: I am having a car, so I can drop you.
analogy: Owning is a still photo. "I'm having lunch" is a video: it's happening now.
tryPrompt: A friend asks if you own a bike. You do. Answer in one sentence.
answer: Yes, I have a bike. It's an old Activa, but it runs.

title: "Am knowing him" → "I've known him"
rule: In global English, say "I've known" for a time up to now.

examples.work: I've known Fatima since our first job, so I'll ask her.
examples.everyday: We've known our neighbours for ten years; they're like family.

insteadOf: I am knowing him for five years.
analogy: A train that left years ago and is still running: that's "I've known".
tryPrompt: Tell a new colleague that you and Rahul met in college and are still friends.
answer: I've known Rahul since college. We're still close.

title: "Have bought yesterday" → "bought"
rule: In global English, a finished time like "yesterday" takes the simple past.

examples.work: I sent the invoice yesterday, so it should reach them today.
examples.everyday: I bought the book yesterday and finished it last night.

insteadOf: I have bought the book yesterday.
analogy: "Yesterday" is a shop with its shutter down: it's closed, so use the plain past.
tryPrompt: Tell your manager the vendor called last Monday. One sentence.
answer: The vendor called last Monday.

title: "Since five years" → "for five years"
rule: In global English, "for" goes with a length; "since" with a start.

examples.work: I've been working here for five years, since 2021.
examples.everyday: We've lived in Pune since 2019, so for about seven years.

insteadOf: I am working here since five years.
analogy: "Since" is the date on the calendar. "For" is how many pages you've turned.
tryPrompt: You started learning the guitar two years ago and still practise. Say it in one sentence.
answer: I've been learning the guitar for two years.

title: "She know" → "she knows"
rule: In global English, he, she or it takes a verb with "-s".

examples.work: Riya knows the payments code best, so ask her.
examples.everyday: My dad watches every match, even the boring ones.

insteadOf: She know JavaScript very well.
analogy: The "-s" is a name badge: he, she and it always wear one.
tryPrompt: Tell your team that Arjun speaks Tamil and can help on the Chennai call.
answer: Arjun speaks Tamil, so he can help on the Chennai call.

title: "Would be" → "will be" for a plan
rule: In global English, "will" states a plan; "would" sounds unsure.

examples.work: The next step will be to test it on Monday.
examples.everyday: Dinner will be at eight, so come by half past seven.

insteadOf: The next step would be to test it.
analogy: "Will" is a confirmed train ticket. "Would" is still on the waiting list.
tryPrompt: In the meeting, say that the next step is a call with the client on Friday.
answer: The next step will be a call with the client on Friday.

title: "Enjoyed very much" → "enjoyed it"
rule: In global English, "enjoy" needs an object: "enjoyed it", "enjoyed ourselves".

examples.work: Thanks for organising the offsite. We really enjoyed it.
examples.everyday: We really enjoyed the food at the wedding, especially the biryani.

insteadOf: The party was great. We enjoyed very much.
analogy: "Enjoy" is an empty plate until you say what's on it.
tryPrompt: A colleague asks if you liked yesterday's team lunch. You loved it. Answer using "enjoy".
answer: I really enjoyed it. The paneer was great.

title: Questions: flip to "are you"
rule: In global English, questions flip the order: "are you", "will you".

examples.work: When will you send the deck?
examples.everyday: Which way are you going? We can share an auto.

insteadOf: Which way you are going?
analogy: A question is a cup turned upside down: "you are" becomes "are you".
tryPrompt: Ask Joseph what time he's leaving for the airport.
answer: What time are you leaving for the airport?

title: "Isn't it?" → the matching tag
rule: In global English, the tag matches the verb: "aren't they?", "don't you?"

examples.work: The client is joining at three, isn't she?
examples.everyday: Your parents are coming tomorrow, aren't they?

insteadOf: They're coming tomorrow, isn't it?
analogy: Like an echo in a well: the tag bounces back the verb you just used.
tryPrompt: Check with Priya that she's coming to the stand-up. End with a short tag.
answer: You're coming to the stand-up, aren't you?

title: "Trainings" → "training sessions"
rule: In global English, "training" and "research" take no plural "-s".

examples.work: We have two training sessions this week.
examples.everyday: My sister is doing research on rice farming.

insteadOf: We have two trainings and some researches this week.
analogy: Like rice: you say "two bowls of rice", never "two rices".
tryPrompt: Tell HR you went to three safety classes this month. Use "training".
answer: I attended three safety training sessions this month.

title: "The alphabets" → "the alphabet"
rule: In global English, "alphabet" means the whole set; each one's a letter.

examples.work: The code uses only letters of the alphabet, no numbers.
examples.everyday: My son can say the whole alphabet now, A to Z.

insteadOf: My son is learning his alphabets.
analogy: The alphabet is the whole deck of cards; each letter is one card.
tryPrompt: Tell a friend your niece knows all 26 letters now.
answer: My niece knows the whole alphabet now.

title: "A master's student in CS"
rule: In global English, say "a master's student in" a subject.

examples.work: I'm a master's student in data science, interning here this summer.
examples.everyday: My cousin is a PhD student in history at Delhi University.

insteadOf: I am master's student of computer science.
analogy: You study in a subject the way you sit in a train: inside it.
tryPrompt: Introduce yourself at a meetup. You're doing a master's in finance.
answer: Hi, I'm Arjun. I'm a master's student in finance.

title: "One book" → "a book"
rule: In global English, use "a", not "one", unless the number matters.

examples.work: A client called about the invoice this morning.
examples.everyday: She gave me a book for my birthday.

insteadOf: She gave me one book to read.
analogy: "One" holds up a finger to count. "A" just points.
tryPrompt: Tell your friend that someone at work told you about a nice café near the office.
answer: A colleague told me about a nice café near the office.

title: "Attention on" → "attention to"
rule: In global English, you pay attention to something, not on it.

examples.work: Please pay attention to the dates on the last slide.
examples.everyday: Pay attention to the road, not your phone.

insteadOf: Please pay attention on the last slide.
analogy: Attention travels to it, like a ball thrown to the keeper.
tryPrompt: Ask the new joiner to focus on the security steps. Use "pay attention".
answer: Please pay attention to the security steps.

title: "Cope up with" → "cope with"
rule: In global English, it's "cope with", with no "up".

examples.work: How do you cope with three projects at once?
examples.everyday: Mum is coping well with the move to Pune.

insteadOf: How do you cope up with so much work?
analogy: The "up" is a second spoon of sugar nobody asked for.
tryPrompt: Ask a colleague how they manage their two-hour commute every day. Use "cope".
answer: How do you cope with that commute every day?

title: "I'm here only" → "I'm right here"
rule: In global English, stress a place with "right": "right here".

examples.work: The file's right here, in the shared folder.
examples.everyday: Don't worry, I'm right here, by the gate.

insteadOf: Where are you? — I'm here only.
analogy: "Right" is a pin on the map: exactly this spot.
tryPrompt: Your friend can't find you at the station. Tell them you're at platform 2, near the tea stall.
answer: I'm right here, on platform 2, near the tea stall.

title: "Small small" → "really small"
rule: In global English, say "really small" or "little", not "small small".

examples.work: These are really small fixes; I'll finish them today.
examples.everyday: Let's not fight over little things.

insteadOf: Let's not fight over small small things.
analogy: Saying "small" twice is two spoons of sugar; "really" is one, and enough.
tryPrompt: Tell your manager the review found only a few tiny typos.
answer: The review found only a few really small typos.

title: "Three-four" → "three or four"
rule: In global English, say "three or four", with "or".

examples.work: Three or four people from sales are joining the call.
examples.everyday: We'll be back in two or three days.

insteadOf: Three-four people are joining the call.
analogy: Like "chai or coffee?" on a menu: "or" means one of the two.
tryPrompt: Your team needs a few more days: maybe two, maybe three. Tell your manager.
answer: We need two or three more days.

title: "Too good" → "really good"
rule: In global English, "too" means more than is OK.

examples.work: Your demo was really good. The client loved it.
examples.everyday: The chai's really good, but too hot to drink yet.

insteadOf: This coffee is too good!
analogy: "Too" is the red zone on a speedometer; "really" is just fast.
tryPrompt: Tell your aunt her dosa is excellent.
answer: Aunty, this dosa is really good!

title: "Expired" → "passed away"
rule: In global English, people "pass away"; milk and passports "expire".

examples.work: Rahul's grandfather passed away, so he's on leave this week.
examples.everyday: Check the milk; I think it expired yesterday.

insteadOf: His grandfather expired last week.
analogy: "Expire" is the date stamped on a packet, not a word for a person.
tryPrompt: Tell your team gently that Joseph is away because his grandmother died.
answer: Joseph's away this week. His grandmother passed away.

title: "Call to my party" → "invite"
rule: In global English, you "invite" people to an event.

examples.work: Let's invite the design team to the launch lunch.
examples.everyday: I'm inviting Riya to my birthday dinner.

insteadOf: I'll call her to my party.
analogy: "Call" is the phone ringing. "Invite" is the card in their hand.
tryPrompt: Tell a colleague you'd like them to come to your housewarming on Sunday.
answer: I'd like to invite you to my housewarming on Sunday.

title: "Cent percent" → "a hundred percent"
rule: In global English, say "a hundred percent" or "one hundred percent".

examples.work: I'm a hundred percent sure the numbers are right.
examples.everyday: She got a hundred percent in maths!

insteadOf: I'm cent percent sure.
analogy: Like "a dozen eggs": the "a" comes first, so "a hundred percent".
tryPrompt: Your manager asks if you're sure about Friday's launch. You're completely sure. Answer.
answer: Yes, I'm a hundred percent sure. We're ready for Friday.

title: "That hotel" → "that restaurant"
rule: In global English, a "hotel" is for staying; a "restaurant" for eating.

examples.work: Let's take the client to that South Indian restaurant.
examples.everyday: We stayed at a hotel in Goa and ate at the beach shacks.

insteadOf: Let's eat lunch at that hotel near the office.
analogy: A hotel gives you a bed; a restaurant gives you a plate.
tryPrompt: Suggest to your friends that you all have dinner at the new biryani place.
answer: Shall we have dinner at that new biryani restaurant?

title: "Mugging" → "cramming"
rule: In global English, say "cramming"; "mugging" usually means robbing.

examples.work: I crammed the new process notes the night before the audit.
examples.everyday: My brother's cramming for his board exams.

insteadOf: I was mugging all night for the exam.
analogy: Cramming is stuffing a suitcase the night before the trip.
tryPrompt: Tell a friend you studied all night just before your driving test.
answer: I crammed all night before my driving test.

title: "Co-brother" → "brother-in-law"
rule: In global English, your wife's sister's husband is your "brother-in-law".

examples.work: I'm off on Friday; my brother-in-law is flying in from Dubai.
examples.everyday: My brother-in-law makes the best biryani in the family.

insteadOf: My co-brother is visiting this weekend.
analogy: One key ring, many keys: "brother-in-law" opens several family doors.
tryPrompt: Tell a colleague your wife's sister's husband is joining you for the match.
answer: My brother-in-law is coming to the match with us.

title: "By-heart it" → "learn it by heart"
rule: In global English, you "learn it by heart" or "memorise" it.

examples.work: I've learned the opening lines of the pitch by heart.
examples.everyday: My daughter memorised the whole poem in a day.

insteadOf: I have to by-heart the whole speech.
analogy: "By heart" is the shelf; "learn" is putting the book on it.
tryPrompt: Tell a friend you need to know your lines for the office skit without the paper.
answer: I need to learn my lines by heart before Friday.

title: "Updation" → "updating"
rule: In global English, say "updating" or "an update", not "updation".

examples.work: Updating the records will take till Friday.
examples.everyday: Can you give me an update on the plumber?

insteadOf: The updation of records is pending.
analogy: "Update" is already a ready-made roti; no need to knead "updation".
tryPrompt: Tell your manager the address changes in the system are still not done.
answer: Updating the addresses is still pending.

title: "Ramu this side" → "Hi, it's Ramu"
rule: In global English, start a phone call with "Hi, it's Ramu."

examples.work: Hi, it's Arjun from the design team. Is now a good time?
examples.everyday: Hi Aunty, it's Riya. Is Mum there?

insteadOf: Hello, Ramu this side.
analogy: "It's Ramu" is your voice knocking: they know who's at the door.
tryPrompt: You're calling a vendor, Meena, for the first time. Open the call.
answer: Hi Meena, it's Rahul from Brightline. Do you have a minute?

title: "Mention not" → "You're welcome"
rule: In global English, answer "thanks" with "You're welcome" or "No problem".

examples.work: "Thanks for covering the call." "No problem, happy to help."
examples.everyday: "Thanks for the lift!" "You're welcome. Anytime."

insteadOf: "Thanks for the help!" — "Mention not."
analogy: "You're welcome" is holding the door open after their thank-you.
tryPrompt: Your neighbour thanks you for watering her plants while she was away. Reply warmly.
answer: You're welcome! Happy to help.

title: "Cut the call" → "hang up"
rule: In global English, you "hang up" or "end the call".

examples.work: Let's end the call here and pick this up tomorrow.
examples.everyday: Don't hang up yet, Mum wants to say hi.

insteadOf: Wait, don't cut the call.
analogy: Old phones hung the receiver on a hook, so the call "hung up".
tryPrompt: Ask your friend to stay on the phone while you find a pen.
answer: Don't hang up, I'm just getting a pen.

title: "Eating my head" → "annoying me"
rule: In global English, say "He's annoying me" or "He's driving me crazy".

examples.work: This printer has been annoying me all morning.
examples.everyday: My brother keeps asking for my phone. He's driving me crazy.

insteadOf: My cousin is eating my head about the trip.
analogy: Said abroad, "eating my head" sounds like a horror film, not a cousin who won't stop asking.
tryPrompt: Your neighbour's dog barks all night. Tell a friend how you feel about it.
answer: The neighbour's dog barks all night. It's driving me crazy.

title: "Duly signed" → "signed"
rule: In global English, "duly" sounds old-fashioned; just drop it.

examples.work: I've attached the signed form.
examples.everyday: I've filled in the school form and dropped it off.

insteadOf: Please find attached the duly signed form.
analogy: "Duly" is a typewriter in a laptop office: it works, but feels old.
tryPrompt: Email HR that your completed joining form is attached.
answer: Hi, I've attached my completed joining form.
